sections.body: Turnaround time=completion−arrival; waiting time=turnaround−CPU burst (when no I/O time is included); response time=first run−arrival.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: With all processes arriving at time 0, bursts P1=4,P2=2,P3=1, nonpreemptive SJF runs P3,P2,P1. Waiting times are 0,1,3; average=4/3.
points: Bursts 3,5 arriving at 0 under FCFS → waits 0,3; average 1.5.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Average waiting = Σwaiting / number of processes
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Do not confuse waiting, response and turnaround; include arrival times and context-switch overhead if provided.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Operating System::Memory Management.subject: Operating System
Operating System::Memory Management.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Memory Management: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Paging splits virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames. A page table maps virtual page numbers to frame numbers; offset bits are preserved.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: A TLB caches address translations. Page faults trigger OS handling when a needed page is absent; replacement policies include FIFO and LRU. Thrashing occurs when excessive faults dominate useful work.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: With 4 KB pages, offset=12 bits. Virtual address 0x12345 has page number 0x12 and offset 0x345; physical address uses the mapped frame number plus 0x345.
points: 4 KiB pages require 12 offset bits for byte addresses.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Effective access time depends on TLB hit/miss path
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Page size determines offset bits, not frame-number bits; a TLB miss is not necessarily a page fault.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Operating System::File Systems.subject: Operating System
Operating System::File Systems.overview: GATE CSE study notes for File Systems: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: A file system maps names to metadata and storage blocks. Inodes or analogous structures store attributes and block pointers; directories map names to file identifiers.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: Contiguous allocation gives efficient sequential access but external fragmentation; linked allocation eases growth but hurts random access; indexed allocation supports direct block lookup.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: For a 12-byte direct-block pointer and 4 KB block size, a file using three direct data blocks stores at most 12 KB of data, excluding metadata. Actual inode limits depend on its pointer layout.
points: A Unix-style inode stores metadata and block pointers, not the filename itself.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Indexed allocation uses an index block or inode pointers
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: File descriptor, inode and filename are different concepts; hard links and symbolic links have different semantics.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Databases::ER Model.subject: Databases
Databases::ER Model.overview: GATE CSE study notes for ER Model: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Entity sets represent objects; attributes describe them; relationships connect entity sets. Cardinality constraints express one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many participation.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: A weak entity depends on an owner entity for identification. Mapping an M:N relationship to tables usually requires a separate relation containing foreign keys to both participating entity tables.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: Student(SID,Name) and Course(CID,Title) with M:N Enrolls become Enrollment(SID,CID,Grade), where (SID,CID) can be a composite key if each enrollment is unique.
points: Department–Employee often modeled 1:N if each employee belongs to one department.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: 1:N relationship: one entity instance can relate to many on other side
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Participation (mandatory/optional) and cardinality (1:N/M:N) answer different questions.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Databases::Relational Model and SQL.subject: Databases
Databases::Relational Model and SQL.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Relational Model and SQL: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: A relation is a set of tuples with attributes; keys uniquely identify tuples. Selection filters rows, projection selects columns and join combines related tuples.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: SQL SELECT-FROM-WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates groups; HAVING filters groups. INNER JOIN keeps matching rows; LEFT JOIN also keeps unmatched left rows with NULLs.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM Employee GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*)>2; returns departments with at least three employees. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) ignores NULL values.
points: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*)>3;

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: σ filters rows; π projects columns; HAVING filters groups
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: SQL uses bag semantics by default; DISTINCT removes duplicates, and comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Databases::Integrity Constraints and Nor.subject: Databases
Databases::Integrity Constraints and Nor.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Integrity Constraints and Normalization: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Integrity constraints include domain rules, primary keys, foreign keys and checks. Functional dependency X→Y means any two tuples agreeing on X must agree on Y.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: 2NF eliminates partial dependency of non-prime attributes on a proper subset of a candidate key; 3NF restricts transitive dependency; BCNF requires every nontrivial FD determinant to be a superkey.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: In Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,StudentName), if StudentID→StudentName and key is (StudentID,CourseID), StudentName depends on only part of the key; split Student(StudentID,StudentName) from Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID).
points: R(A,B,C), A→B, B→C: A is a candidate key; B→C violates BCNF.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: BCNF: for every nontrivial FD X→Y, X is a superkey
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Normalization aims to reduce anomalies; a lossless decomposition and dependency preservation are separate properties.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Databases::File Organization and Indexin.subject: Databases
Databases::File Organization and Indexin.overview: GATE CSE study notes for File Organization and Indexing: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Heap files store records without sorted key order; sorted files support ordered access but insertion can be expensive. Hash file organization uses a hash function to choose buckets.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: A B+ tree keeps search keys in internal nodes and record references at leaves, with leaves linked for range scans. Dense indexes may have an entry per search-key value or record depending on definition; sparse indexes sample blocks.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: For an index on salary, SELECT ... WHERE salary BETWEEN 30000 AND 50000 can use a B+ tree range scan. A hash index is efficient for equality but not ordered ranges.
points: A B+ tree range query scans consecutive leaf entries after locating start.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: B+ tree keeps record pointers typically at leaves; internal nodes guide search
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: A clustered index determines physical or logical record ordering; distinguish index height from number of records scanned.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Databases::Transactions and Concurrency.subject: Databases
Databases::Transactions and Concurrency.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Transactions and Concurrency Control: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: A transaction groups operations with ACID properties: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. COMMIT makes changes permanent; ROLLBACK cancels uncommitted work.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: Conflict serializability can be tested using a precedence graph; a cycle means the schedule is not conflict-serializable. Two-phase locking grows then shrinks lock holdings and ensures conflict serializability, but can deadlock.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: Schedule R1(X),W1(X),R2(X),W2(X) has T1→T2 conflict edges. If another item creates T2→T1, the precedence graph has a cycle and schedule is not conflict-serializable.
points: If T1 writes X before T2 reads X, precedence edge T1→T2.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Conflict-serializable iff precedence graph is acyclic
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Serializable does not mean transactions literally run one after another; distinguish recoverability, cascadelessness and strictness.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Computer Networks::Network Layering and.subject: Computer Networks
Computer Networks::Network Layering and.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Network Layering and Switching: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Layering separates concerns: application protocols use transport services; transport uses network delivery; link protocols move frames across one hop. Encapsulation adds headers at successive layers.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: Circuit switching reserves a path or resources for a connection; packet switching forwards independent packets and shares links statistically. Store-and-forward switches receive a packet before transmitting it onward.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: A 1000-byte packet on a 1 Mbps link takes 8000/10^6=0.008 seconds=8 ms to serialize, excluding propagation and queueing.
points: 1000-bit frame at 1 Mbps takes 1 ms to transmit.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Transmission delay=L/R; propagation delay=d/s
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Transmission delay is packet bits/link rate; propagation delay is distance/signal speed. Do not interchange them.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Computer Networks::Data Link Layer and E.subject: Computer Networks
Computer Networks::Data Link Layer and E.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Data Link Layer and Ethernet: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: The data-link layer frames packets, detects errors and coordinates medium access. CRC uses polynomial division to detect many bit-error patterns; it does not generally correct errors.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: Ethernet frames carry source/destination MAC addresses. Switches learn source MAC-to-port mappings and forward known unicasts to one port, flooding unknown unicasts within a VLAN.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: If a switch learns host A on port 1 and host B on port 2, a frame from A to B is forwarded only to port 2 after B's location is known.
points: Parity bit detects any odd number of bit errors, not all even errors.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: CRC uses modulo-2 polynomial division
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: MAC addresses operate at link layer, IP addresses at network layer; collisions and broadcast domains are different concepts.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Computer Networks::Routing Algorithms.subject: Computer Networks
Computer Networks::Routing Algorithms.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Routing Algorithms: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Distance-vector routing exchanges distance estimates with neighbors and is related to Bellman-Ford. Link-state routing floods topology information and computes shortest paths with Dijkstra.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: A router's forwarding table selects the next hop using destination prefix matching. Routing protocols compute paths; forwarding applies the table to each packet.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: If route A→B costs 2 and B→C costs 3, A's route via B to C costs 5. A direct route cost 8 is worse, assuming additive link costs.
points: Router uses next hop from forwarding table, not full end-to-end path in packet.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Dijkstra computes shortest paths for nonnegative edge weights
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Distance-vector protocols can experience count-to-infinity; shortest paths depend on metrics, not merely hop count.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Computer Networks::IPv4, CIDR and NAT.subject: Computer Networks
Computer Networks::IPv4, CIDR and NAT.overview: GATE CSE study notes for IPv4, CIDR and NAT: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: IPv4 addresses have 32 bits. CIDR /p means p prefix bits and 32−p host bits; a subnet has 2^(32−p) addresses before special-address considerations.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: Longest-prefix matching selects the most specific matching route. NAT translates private addresses/ports to public ones, often allowing multiple internal hosts to share one public address.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: 192.168.1.130/26 belongs to subnet 192.168.1.128/26; the block size is 64 addresses, from .128 through .191.
points: 192.168.1.0/26 covers .0–.63; typical usable hosts .1–.62.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: IPv4 /26 subnet has 2^(32−26)=64 addresses
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Do not confuse subnet address count with usable host count; point-to-point and special prefixes have exceptions.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Computer Networks::TCP.subject: Computer Networks
Computer Networks::TCP.overview: GATE CSE study notes for TCP: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission and flow control. It is connection-oriented and typically starts with a three-way handshake.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: Flow control limits sender data based on receiver-advertised window; congestion control adjusts sending based on perceived network congestion. RTT and retransmission timeout influence recovery.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: If sender transmits bytes with sequence numbers 1000–1499, the next expected ACK is 1500 (assuming all bytes arrive in order). ACKs refer to the next expected byte, not packet count.
points: Window 64 KiB and RTT 0.1 s gives about 655360 bytes/s.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Window-limited throughput approximately window/RTT when no other bottleneck
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: TCP preserves byte order, not application message boundaries; flow control and congestion control are different mechanisms.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

Computer Networks::DNS and HTTP.subject: Computer Networks
Computer Networks::DNS and HTTP.overview: GATE CSE study notes for DNS and HTTP: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: DNS resolves names to records such as A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), MX (mail exchange) and CNAME (alias). Recursive resolvers cache answers according to TTL.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: HTTP uses request methods such as GET, POST, PUT and DELETE with status codes. HTTPS runs HTTP over TLS to provide authenticated encrypted transport under normal validation.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: A browser may resolve example.com to an IP address, establish TCP/TLS, send GET / and receive 200 OK with a response body. A 404 means the requested resource was not found.
points: HTTP GET retrieves a representation; DNS resolves a name before connection when uncached.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: DNS A record maps hostname to IPv4 address
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: DNS does not itself transfer webpage content; HTTP is stateless at protocol level, with cookies/sessions providing continuity.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

General Aptitude::Verbal Aptitude.subject: General Aptitude
General Aptitude::Verbal Aptitude.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Verbal Aptitude: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Reading comprehension asks for main idea, inference and author attitude. An inference must follow from the passage rather than outside assumptions.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: Sentence correction tests subject-verb agreement, tense, parallelism, modifiers and pronoun reference. Vocabulary questions depend on context rather than memorized isolated meanings.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: Sentence 'Each of the students are ready' is corrected to 'Each of the students is ready' because the head subject each is singular.
points: “Neither of the answers is correct” uses singular verb in formal agreement.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Use context and grammatical agreement to eliminate options
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Avoid extreme options in inference questions unless the passage explicitly supports them; check grammar around the actual subject.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

General Aptitude::Quantitative Aptitude.subject: General Aptitude
General Aptitude::Quantitative Aptitude.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Quantitative Aptitude: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Percentages describe ratios per hundred; a percentage change is (new−old)/old×100. Successive percentage changes multiply their factors rather than add directly.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: Speed=distance/time; work rates add when workers operate independently; compound interest uses A=P(1+r)^n for annual compounding at rate r.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: A price rises 20% then falls 20%: final factor=1.2×0.8=0.96, so net change is a 4% decrease, not zero.
points: Price 200→250 means 25% increase.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Percentage change=(new−old)/old ×100
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Distinguish percentage points from percent change; verify units and whether interest is simple or compounded.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

General Aptitude::Analytical Aptitude.subject: General Aptitude
General Aptitude::Analytical Aptitude.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Analytical Aptitude: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Analytical reasoning includes ordering, constraints, deductions and data interpretation. Translate statements into explicit variables and logical constraints before trying cases.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: For arrangement puzzles, draw slots and apply definite conditions first. For syllogisms, distinguish universal statements, existence claims and invalid converses.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: If A is before B and B is before C, transitivity implies A is before C. But 'all A are B' does not imply 'all B are A'.
points: All A are B; all B are C ⇒ all A are C.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Valid inference: if P→Q and P, then Q
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Do not assume unstated existence from a universal claim; a single counterexample invalidates a universal deduction.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.

General Aptitude::Spatial Aptitude.subject: General Aptitude
General Aptitude::Spatial Aptitude.overview: GATE CSE study notes for Spatial Aptitude: concepts, explanations, solved reasoning, formulas and exam traps.

sections.heading: Core concept and meaning
sections.body: Spatial aptitude involves mentally rotating shapes, recognizing mirror reflections, folding nets and counting hidden or visible components. A rotation preserves orientation, lengths and adjacency; reflection reverses handedness.
points: Identify what the concept represents and the conditions under which it applies.

sections.heading: Important subtopics and how they work
sections.body: For cube nets, identify opposite faces by folding relationships; faces sharing an edge in the net cannot become opposite. In counting cubes, systematically classify corners, edges, faces and interior positions.
points: Compare related ideas by their definitions and operational behavior.

sections.heading: Worked explanation and example
sections.body: A 3×3×3 cube made of unit cubes has 27 small cubes. If its outside is painted, exactly one interior cube has zero painted faces, while eight corner cubes have three painted faces.
points: A square rotated 90° retains side lengths and area.

sections.heading: Key formula or rule
sections.body: Rotation preserves lengths and angles
points: Check assumptions, boundary cases and units before applying a rule.

sections.heading: Common GATE traps and exam approach
sections.body: Do not confuse a mirror image with a 180-degree rotation; use invariant adjacency and face orientation to eliminate options.
points: For numerical questions, write known values and assumptions before substitution.
For conceptual MCQs, test edge cases and counterexamples.
